Slide 1. Modules, Packages, and O O P.

Welcome to Module 6. In this module, we are going to learn how to organize Python code as our programs become larger. Up to this point, many of our examples have been small enough to fit inside one script or one notebook. That is fine when the program is short. But as an analytics project grows, we may have many helper functions, calculations, reports, and repeated tasks. At that point, organization becomes important.

Python gives us several ways to organize our work. We can use modules to reuse code from another Python file. We can use packages to group related modules. We can also use classes and objects to keep related data and behavior together.

The goal of this module is not advanced software engineering. The goal is to understand a few practical tools that make analytical code easier to reuse, test, explain, and grow.

Slide 3. Learning path for Module 6.

This module has six main parts.

First, we will look at imports and learn how Python can use built-in tools from other modules.

Second, we will create our own module and see how one Python file can provide reusable functions to another file.

Third, we will connect the ideas of modules, packages, and libraries. This will help prepare us for later modules where we use NumPy and Pandas.

Fourth, we will introduce classes. A class is a blueprint for creating objects.

Fifth, we will create objects and methods, and we will learn what the word self means inside a class.

Finally, we will compare functions, dictionaries, modules, packages, classes, and objects so that we can choose the simplest tool that fits a task.

Slide 4. Why organize code?

Small scripts are easy to manage at the beginning. But analytics projects usually grow. We may clean data, calculate several metrics, create charts, generate reports, and repeat the same steps for different datasets.

If all of that code stays inside one very long file, it becomes harder to find a specific function. It also becomes easier to accidentally change something that breaks another part of the program.

A more organized project gives related work a clear home. For example, data-cleaning functions could go in one file. Metric calculations could go in another file. Chart functions could go in another file. A main script could then bring those pieces together.

Organization is also useful for teamwork. Clear file names and clear structure make code easier for other people to review. It also helps your future self. Code that is well organized today will be much easier to understand when you return to it several weeks or months later.

Slide 5. What is a module?

A module is a Python file that contains code we can use somewhere else.

A simple way to think about a module is to imagine a toolbox. The toolbox contains tools. We import the toolbox, and then we use the tools inside it.

For example, Python includes a built-in module called math. When we write import math, Python gives our program access to the functions and constants inside that module.

If we then write math dot square root with the value eighty-one, Python uses the square root function stored inside the math module.

The module name also helps organize the code. When we see math dot square root, we immediately know that the square root function came from the math module.

Slide 7. Aliases and selective imports.

Python gives us more than one way to import code.

The first style is to import the whole module. For example, import math. This is useful when we want to use several tools from the same module.

The second style is to use an alias. An alias gives a module a shorter name. For example, import statistics as stats. After that, we can write stats dot mean instead of statistics dot mean.

Aliases are especially common in data analytics. Later, you will often see NumPy imported as N P and Pandas imported as P D.

The third style is a selective import. For example, from math import square root. This brings in only one specific function.

The main goal is readability. Use an alias when it makes the code easier to read. Avoid creating short or confusing names that make the code harder to understand.

Slide 9. Create your own module.

Modules are not limited to the tools that come with Python. We can create our own modules.

Imagine that we have a project folder with two files. One file is called calculations dot P Y. The other file is called main dot P Y.

The calculations file can contain reusable formulas, such as a function that calculates profit. The main file can focus on the analysis itself and import the functions it needs from calculations.

This creates a useful separation. The reusable formulas have one clear home, while the main analysis remains shorter and easier to read.

A good beginner rule is this. When one script starts to contain many reusable functions, consider moving related functions into their own module file.

Slide 11. What is a package?

A package is a folder that groups related Python modules together.

Remember the basic distinction. A module is usually one P Y file. A package is a folder that contains related modules.

For example, an analytics project could contain separate modules for cleaning, metrics, and charts. Those related files could be grouped together inside one package folder.

Packages help keep a project from turning into one very long file or one crowded folder.

At this stage, you do not need to build a complex Python package. The important goal is to recognize the idea and understand why packages are useful when projects become larger.

Slide 12. Module, package, and library.

The words module, package, and library are related, but they are not exactly the same.

A module is one Python file that contains reusable code. For example, math is a module, and a file that we create called calculations dot P Y can also be a module.

A package is a folder that groups related modules together.

A library is a larger collection of reusable tools. A library may contain several packages and modules.

Later in the course, we will work with NumPy and Pandas. Those are examples of large reusable libraries that provide many tools for data analysis.

A simple rule to remember is this. Module means file. Package means folder. Library means a larger collection of reusable tools.

Slide 14. What is a class?

Now we move from modules and packages to object-oriented programming.

A class is a blueprint. It describes what information an object should store and what actions that object can perform.

For example, imagine a class named Sale. The class could describe the information that every sale should have, such as an item name, a price, and a quantity. It could also describe actions, such as calculating the total value of the sale.

The class itself is only the blueprint. When we use the class to create one specific sale, that specific item is called an object.

The simple idea is that a class keeps related data and related behavior together.

Slide 15. Code: create a simple class.

This code creates a class named Customer Record.

Inside the class, we define a special method called dunder init. The written version has two underscores before and after the word init. You can simply remember its spoken name as dunder init.

Dunder init runs when a new object is created. In this example, it receives a customer identification value and a segment.

The lines self dot customer I D and self dot segment store those values inside the new object.

Next, the code creates one object named customer. It uses the Customer Record class and gives the object the values C one zero one and Retail.

Finally, the program prints the two attributes stored in the object.

Click Run. The terminal should show the customer identification and the segment.

The word self is important. Self refers to the current object. In this example, self dot customer I D means the customer identification that belongs to this particular customer object.

As a small practice, create a second customer object with a different identification value and segment, then print its attributes.

Slide 16. One class can create many objects.

A class is a blueprint, not a single object.

The same class can create many different objects. Each object can store its own values.

For example, one Product class can create a laptop object and a monitor object. Both objects follow the same Product blueprint, but one object can have a price of nine hundred dollars while another object has a price of three hundred dollars.

This is one reason classes are useful. We define the structure and behavior once, and then we create as many objects as we need.

The simple idea is this. Same blueprint. Different objects. Different values.

This code defines a Product class.

The dunder init method stores a product name and a price inside each object.

The class also contains a method named sale price. This method receives a discount rate and calculates a discounted price using the object's own price.

Next, the program creates two objects. Item one represents a laptop with a price of nine hundred dollars. Item two represents a monitor with a price of three hundred dollars.

The code prints the regular price and a ten percent discounted price for each object.

Click Run. In the terminal, you should see separate results for the laptop and the monitor.

Notice that both objects use exactly the same class and the same sale price method. The difference is that each object stores its own name and price.

Try creating a third Product object with a different name and price. Then call the sale price method for that new object.

Slide 18. Methods and self.

A method is a function that belongs to a class.

Methods describe actions that objects can perform. For example, a Sale object might have a method named total that calculates price multiplied by quantity.

Inside a method, we usually use self to access the data stored in the current object.

For example, self dot price means the price stored in this particular object. Self dot quantity means the quantity stored in this object.

An attribute is data stored in an object. A method is an action that belongs to the object. Self refers to the current object.

This connection between attributes, methods, and self is one of the most important ideas in basic object-oriented programming.

Slide 19. Code: add behavior with a method.

This code defines a Sale class.

The dunder init method stores three pieces of information inside each Sale object. Those values are item, price, and quantity.

The class also contains a method named total. The total method multiplies self dot price by self dot quantity and returns the result.

The program then creates one Sale object for a notebook. The price is twelve dollars and fifty cents, and the quantity is four.

The final lines print the item name, the quantity, and the total value.

Click Run. The terminal should show a total of fifty dollars.

Notice how the total method does not need us to pass the price and quantity again. The method already has access to the values stored inside that particular object through self.

When a Sales Report object is created, the dunder init method stores a list of sales values inside the object.

The class contains three methods.

The total sales method adds all of the sales values.

The average sale method calculates the average of the values.

The high sales count method receives a cutoff value. It loops through the stored sales and counts how many values are greater than or equal to that cutoff.

This example shows when a class can be useful in analytics. The object stores a dataset, and the methods provide several calculations that belong to that dataset.

Slide 21. Function, dictionary, or class?

At this point, you may wonder whether you should use a function, a dictionary, or a class.

The best beginner rule is to use the simplest structure that clearly matches the job.

Use a function when you mainly need to perform one reusable task. For example, a get profit function can receive sales and costs and return profit.

Use a dictionary when you mainly need to store related values. For example, a product dictionary could store a name and a price.

Use a class when data and repeated behavior belong together. For example, a Product class can store a product's name and price and also contain a method for calculating a discounted price.

Do not use a class just because classes exist. Start simple. Move to a class when one concept naturally has both stored data and repeated actions.

Slide 22. Choosing the right organization tool.

This slide summarizes the main organization tools from the module.

A function is best for one reusable task.

A module is best when you have a file of related functions or constants.

A package is useful when a project has several related modules that should be grouped together.

A class is useful when data and behavior belong together.

An object is one actual instance created from a class.

A practical workflow is to start with functions. When one file becomes long, move related functions into modules. When several modules belong together, group them into a package. Use a class when one real concept has both data and actions that belong together.

The goal is not to make the project more complicated. The goal is to make the code easier to understand.

Slide 23. Module 6 wrap-up.

We have reached the end of Module 6.

The first major idea is modules. Modules let us import reusable tools instead of rewriting the same code.

The second idea is packages. Packages group related modules when a project becomes larger.

The third idea is classes. Classes provide a blueprint for keeping related data and behavior together.

We also learned that one class can create many objects. Each object can store its own values while using the same methods.

A useful practice activity is to create a Student Score class. Give the class a student name and a list of scores. Then add a method that calculates the average score. Create two different objects and print the average for each one.

The main skill from this module is not memorizing every line of syntax. The main skill is recognizing when your analytical code is becoming large enough that better organization will make it easier to reuse, test, explain, and maintain.

In the next module, we will continue building our Python skills with more advanced programming techniques.
